title: The five-minute reset
description: Between one part of the day and the next, five deliberate minutes can clear stress better than an evening of half-resting.

body.heading: Stress leaks across the borders of the day
paragraphs: Without a border, the morning’s difficult call follows you into lunch, and work follows you home in your shoulders. We imagine we will decompress later, all at once, in the evening — but later we are usually too tired to do anything but collapse into a screen, and the leak continues.
A reset is a small border ritual: five minutes, at a natural seam in the day, spent deliberately clearing the previous chapter before starting the next.

body.heading: What five minutes can hold
paragraphs: Stand up and move — stairs, corridor, around the block. Movement is the fastest legal way to change your state, because stress is partly physical and the body believes what it does. Add daylight if you possibly can.

Then one clearing act: splash cold water, tidy the desk surface, write the three dangling thoughts onto paper, change your shirt, make tea properly. The act itself matters less than its meaning: that chapter is closed, this one starts fresh.

body.heading: Place resets where the seams already are
paragraphs: After the commute, before the meeting block, at the school gate, between work and home — the day is full of natural seams. Choose one to start with and guard its five minutes like an appointment with someone you respect.
Five minutes will not fix an unsustainable workload, and it is not meant to. It is maintenance for the borders of an ordinary day, and ordinary days are where most of life happens.

takeaway: At the seams of the day, spend five minutes closing one chapter before opening the next.
